Course Description
Probability calculus; random variables, their probability distributions and expected values; t, F and chi-square sampling distributions; estimation; testing of hypothesis; and regression analysis with applications.


Assessments

Projects: Four group projects (2-3 people/group) will be assigned throughout the semester.
Exams: There will be 2 exams during the semester. Each exam will have a closed-book and open-book portion. More details will be provided in class.
Final: To be announced in class

title: Midterm
text:
Student’s t distribution is widely used in many areas of statistics. For \(\nu\) degrees of freedom, the probability density function is given by the following:
\[
f(x)=\frac{\Gamma(\frac{\nu+1}{2})}{\sqrt{\pi\nu}\Gamma(\frac\nu 2)}(1+\frac{x^2}{\nu})^{-\frac{\nu+1}{2}}; \quad x\in(-\infty,\infty)
\]

Create a function in R called my_dt to calculate \(f(x)\) at a given \(x\) and \(\nu\).


my_dt <- function(x, nu) {
  fx <- FUNCTION HERE
  return(fx)
}


R has a built in t distribution density function, dt(), that you can use to verify your solution to (1). Evaluate both your function and dt() at the following values of x and \(\nu\) and arrange your results into a neatly formatted table.

\(x=-1.5, \nu=6\)
\(x=0.7, \nu=20\)
\(x=2, \nu=4\)

title: Final Project
text:
The final project for this course consists of two components where you will find and describe a probability distribution that has not been discussed in class (examples). In groups of 2-3, you are tasked with a written report and a presentation of your chosen distribution. All group members are required to equally contribute. Please let your instructor know if you are having issues with non-participation.
Once you and your group have selected a distribution, create a discussion post on Canvas to let the class know which distribution you have selected. Duplicate distributions will not be allowed and will be given to the group who posted first.

title: Final Project
text:
Write-up
Due date: end of the scheduled final exam for the course
The written report should be 4-6 pages and contain the following sections:

Introduction: describe your distribution, the type of data it describes, history, etc.
Mathematical description: provide the mathematical definition of the probability function (you do not need to derive anything), as well as restrictions on the support of the RV and its parameters. Describe the mean and variance of the function (again, you do not need to derive this). Additionally, include a plot of the pmf/pdf, as well as how it changes with different parameters (e.g., the exponential distribution with \(\beta=1,2,3\))
R Implementation: describe how to use this probability function in R (e.g., qnorm(), pnorm(), packages, etc.). If this function is not implemented in R, describe the process of how to write these functions for your distribution.
Applications: describe 2-3 practical applications where your probability function would be used.
Example: provide a completed example of a practical application of the distribution from a published source. If you would like, you may also fit this distribution to data of your own choosing.

title: Final Project
text:
Presentation
Due date: last week of classes
During the last week of classes, you and your group will present your distribution to the class (approximately 4 groups/day). Your presentation should be between 7 and 10 minutes, and include the opportunities for the class to ask questions. At the minimum, you must include the following sections:

Introduction (including mathematical description)
R Implementation
Example

To ensure that each group has enough time to present, a portion of your grade is allocated to keeping your presentation to under 10 minutes.
In addition to presenting your distribution, you are also responsible for listening to your peers present. On Canvas, there is a quiz with one question per group.

title: Homework 1
text:
Complete each of the following problems. You may either type up your solutions or provide a scan of handwritten work. Solutions without work shown are not eligible for credit.

How many different permutations are there of the letters A, B, C, D, E, F for which

A and B are next to each other
E is not last in line

A committee of 6 people is to be chosen from a group consisting of 7 men and 8 women. How any different committees are possible?
Following question 3, if at least 3 women and at least 2 men are required, how many different committees are possible?
Suppose that two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard 52-card deck (no jokers). Let \(A\) be the event that at least one spade is drawn, and let \(B\) be the event that at least one queen is drawn. Are \(A\) and \(B\) independent?
